display_title: Official Review of Paper2664 by Reviewer gMwn

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper aims at measuring the alignment of a CNN with a structured ontology. It uses a pre-trained CNN architecture for computer vision, and assigns structured semantic roles to a subset U of its neural units of the last layers. As the ontology introduces semantic relations between concepts the NN is enabled to cluster topologically related units into semantically rich and meaningful neural circuits.
The evaluation shows the difference between the IoU measure and the newly introduced sigma measure as well as the accuracy effects if neural circuits that are aligned to ontological concepts of the Broden and ImageNet dataset are removed.
 
The paper contributes:
An ontology on top of the Broden dataset where relations are defined without using additional annotations by including hypernymy semantic relations.
A developed metric or probabilistic formulation (score function sigma) of the interaction between neural activations and semantic concepts
Derived from the IOU measure of (Bau et al. 2017) to be independent from the popularity of a concept in the dataset.
Alignment of the neural units with multiple concepts.
For every unit u, sigma yields the relation to every individual concept and concept of families and therefore shows the most related semantic classes.
--> Increased interpretability
content.main_review:
Strength:
Idea to use ontological descriptions and relations to improve the similarity measure between the neural units and the concepts given by the labels of the dataset
Similarity measure is independent to the amount of data (popularity) of the concept/class.
 
Code is available online to reproduce the experiments.
Dataset extension with ontological concepts is also available online.
 
Weaknesses:
The contributions are quite limited, when compared to previous works:
Bau et al. 2017 already proposed the framework to measure the similarity between neural units u and label concepts.
Zhou et al. 2018, proposed the idea to measure the dependency between neural units and label units through accuracy drop.
Therefore the paper only contributes the idea that concepts have a relation given by the ontology.
But is the semantic relation really reflected in the visual domain or just the visual relations?
The evaluation does not provide clear insights in why the new metric is better then the old IoU.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Using auxiliary information in form of an ontology seems to be a promising research direction. However, based on the evaluations it is not clear how the metric benefits from the concept relations of the ontology. It would be from interest to better explain why the idea of unifying concepts in an ontology improves the interpretability.
 
Therefore, the paper needs to rework on grounding the key message of the paper with a more precise evaluation.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.title: Review Response
content.comment:
*Innovation*

For what concerns the innovation brought by our paper, we consider the introduction of semantic relations as a starting point that led us to different improvements. More in general, the use of an ontology required us to design a measure not affected by popularity, which characterizes more general concepts, and polysemy, which we observed to consistently emerge. Furthermore, our framework can align units with rare and even non-annotated concepts by exploiting semantic relations. Quantitatively, in Table 1, the non-leaves row mostly accounts for visual concepts that the framework inferred from ontological information. For instance, in AlexNet we found several units aligned to high-level visual concepts that were not present in Broden, such as “body of water” (7 units), “geological formation” (6 units), or “garment” (5 units). This alignment information could not have been obtained with previous techniques without further dataset annotation, and it is more significant considering that our measure is not prone to award general and popular concepts.

*Visual/semantic relation*

Considering the point about semantic and visual relations, our approach builds on the assumption that the extension of a concept, mediated by visual representation, is sufficient to uniquely identify the concept itself. Many philosophical points of view openly contest this referential-based theory of meaning. Nonetheless, this assumption is implicit in the machine learning models that we are trying to interpret, namely the CNNs used in our paper and by a great deal of the machine vision community. Consequently, we do not require additional assumptions over the relation between concepts and their portrayal in a dataset. Please, feel free to correct us if you intended something different.

*Measurement comparison*

Concerning the evaluation of the newly defined measure, we are currently running additional experiments. We will post the results here as soon as they are available.

*Interpretability improvement*

Finally, while it is not in the scope of the paper to describe a complete interpretative methodology, we will enhance the description of possible applications enabled by our approach. Other than improving the overall semantic alignment, by selecting more precise concepts from a wider pool, we believe that the ontology may improve the interpretative experience. As an example, the role of neural circuits enables a statistical analysis of the most affected classes. With our approach, a user might interpret the circuit at different levels of complexity according to its requirements. In the medical domain, for instance, it might be possible to deliver interpretations at different levels of detail to the patient and to the clinical practitioner. We will improve the conclusive section of the paper by acknowledging similar applications and scenarios.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript provides a novel semantic alignment framework that builds on aligning a structured ontology with the distributed neural representations to further characterize neural representations and semantic concepts and their interrelatedness.  A propagation strategy is defined to align units with concepts that lack an explicit annotation in the alignment dataset. Then the author(s) defined a novel semantic alignment measure acknowledging polysemy in neural units. Finally, this manuscript introduces an algorithm to identify connected neural circuits composed of units aligned to semantically related concepts.
content.main_review:
* Strengths:
This manuscript proposes a novel semantic alignment framework by introducing a way to align a structured ontology with distributed neural representations. Some interesting experimental results are also well demonstrated. 

* Weaknesses:
There is no in-depth comparison of the proposed framework with previously known work.  Section 2 needs to be further clarified.  It is still hard to judge whether the framework is an improvement on previous work.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This is a well-written paper having some interesting results. A few minor revision are list below.
* The idea of aligning a structured ontology with neural representations is interesting. However, the methods and theoretical innovations are still not sufficient. The author(s) must dig deeper into the innovation points before the article can be accepted.
* The literature review is weak. Related work has not been investigated sufficiently before presenting the author’s framework.

content.comment:
*Baseline*

We are currently running additional experiments to improve the comparison between our framework and the original Network Dissection approach. We will publish the results here as soon as they are available.

*Related Works*

Furthermore, we plan to expand and deepen the related works section, addressing the concerns expressed by R3 and other reviewers. We can also anticipate the discussion here if the reviewer feels that this is relevant to the discussion.

*Innovation*

Considering the last concern, in the following, we highlight and clarify what we believe to be the fundamental innovative points of our work and their possible applications. Briefly, these are:

- A broadening of the set of alignable concepts thanks to the ontology and the associated propagation of alignment beyond the hand-labeled concepts.
- The design of a measure that is not affected by popularity, which characterizes more general concepts, and polysemy, which we observed to consistently emerge.
- The introduction of a strategy to highlight clusters of semantically related units and a consequent empirical analysis on different CNNs.
- The possibility of analyzing networks at different levels of generality for different users according to their specific requirements.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2664 by Reviewer Vej2

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims at proposing an approach for the semantic alignment of neural networks units and human-level concepts in the same vein as the work of [Bau et al, 2017]  and their network dissection approach. Compared to previous work, the authors constrain the alignment with an ontology, i.e. concepts and their relations thus providing a semantic alignment measure and a  new interpretation and inspection approach based on neural circuit coherence. Experimental validation of the approach is done on the Broden dataset and its extended version.
content.main_review:
**Strenghs**

+ The idea of using ontology-driven semantic alignment is very interested in the context of neuron units interpretability. Indeed,  it contributes to advancing the understanding of deep neural models which is of prime importance for their deployment.  The proposed approach can be seen as an improvement of the Network Dissection approach [Bau et al, 2017] by constraining and exploiting a structured knowledge between semantic concepts, represented as an ontology. As it is usual to represent domain knowledge in the form of ontology, it seems a good way to improve semantic alignment.
+ The paper is well written.
+ Results on the Broden dataset are promising

**Weaknessess and main concerns**

+ Several references are missing in the related work section both in order to better position the proposed approach compared to other neural network understanding approaches. For instance, how is the approach compared to concept activation vectors  (Kim et al) and their extension? How is the approach position compared to approaches that have shown the importance of semantics in deep neural networks?  I also suggest to the authors to have a deep look at the literature on ontology matching and alignment. 
+ One of the strong hypothesis of the proposed approach is the availability of a pixel-level annotated dataset. How to relax this hypothesis ? What is the behavior of the approach in the case of a noisy annotated dataset and thus a noisy concept mask ?
+ Some strong formalization is needed. For instance, in the equation of section 3.1, an implication relation is used. On the ontology and domain representation level, implication relation has well-defined semantics. Moreover, this equation (1) should be more discussed since the second part of the equation is closer to a mereology relation than a hypernymy relation.
+ A deeper discussion on the relation between semantic similarity and visual similarity is needed since that paper assumes a strong correlation.
+ What about the semantics of the semantic relation s ? 
+ The results of Figure 3 is not so clear and coherence and a measure on the similarity between the extracted concepts could be important additional information.
+ What is the behavior of the approach with different semantic measures than the Jian and Conrath ?
+ What brings the circuit in term of interpretation ?
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach is interesting but can be seen as an improvement of the network dissection approach by constraining high-level concepts with an ontology.   Although interesting, the novelty of the approach is limited and based on very strong assumptions that are not sufficiently discussed. Moreover, the approach lacks a more solid foundation in the area of ontology alignment.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2664 by Reviewer Vej2

content.title: Review Response
content.comment:
*Related Works*

Firstly, we will update our paper with a more comprehensive related work section, rephrasing a discussion of similar techniques that we already acknowledged but cut off because of page constraints. We will make sure to deepen our take on ontology matching approaches. We can also anticipate the discussion here if the reviewer feels that this is relevant to the discussion.

*Noisy Concept Masks*

Concerning the noisy concept masks, we dealt with them empirically by analyzing the same models with a selection of annotated bounding boxes from ImageNet. Because of the page constraints, we relegated these results to Appendix B with a brief link in the main body of the work. We will highlight this more clearly in the text, explicitly acknowledging that bounding boxes approximate concept masks.

*Formalization and visual/semantic correlation*

We are grateful for the suggestion concerning the formalization of the equation in Section 3.1. We will clarify it by highlighting the role and the relation between a concept, its extension, and its portrayal. Essentially, our approach builds on the assumption that the concept extension, mediated by visual representation, is sufficient to identify the concept itself and thus to align it to a neural unit. Many philosophical points of view openly contest this referential-based theory of meaning. Nonetheless, this assumption is implicit in the machine learning models that we are trying to interpret, namely the CNNs used in our paper and by a great deal of the machine vision community. We hope that this also sufficiently answers your subsequent concern about the relation between conceptual meaning and visual data. Anyhow, we will make sure to clearly state this assumption in the paper.

*Semantic relations*

Given an ontology as an extensional relational structure, in our formalization, a semantic relation is a function from concepts to truth values. We acknowledge that we did not sufficiently discuss this in the paper, and we will provide a more thorough characterization.

*Figure 3*

In Figure 3, we wished to highlight the differences between IoU and our probabilistic measure by analyzing an arbitrary unit. Given the examples maximizing the unit, we notice how the IoU, as expected because of its dependence on popularity, selects more general concepts. Our coherence measurement (Equation 9) refers instead to whole circuits, which are not dealt with in Figure 3. Anyhow, we measured the pair-wise Lin similarity between the top-5 aligned concepts for the same unit with IoU (0.438) and concept-likelihood (0.375). This is reasonable since similarity measures depend on the hypernymy induced taxonomy, thus they produce higher responses for different but more general concepts. The top-5 concepts obtained by IoU are more general than those obtained by our measure, as expected and quantified in Table 1, anyhow we will also report the average depth for the top-5 (6.4 for IoU, 8 for ours) to highlight this in Figure 3.

*Similarity measures*

Concerning similarity measures, the Jiang-Conrath similarity is only of the many others included in our implementation. We plan to upload an updated version of the additional Jupyter Notebook that more intuitively guides the user into changing them. The included similarity measures depend on the taxonomy and are inherited by WordNet. Because of this, even different measures provide similar results. In the upcoming version of the paper, we will report runs of the circuits retrieval algorithm with other similarity measures.

*Interpretability improvement*

Finally, ontology-derived neural circuits provide a way to identify subsets of units that the network employs to fulfill semantically related tasks. Furthermore, aligning neurons to concepts within an ontology enables the generation of different explanations at different levels of abstraction/detail for different users, depending on their knowledge or skills. Nonetheless, while the work does not focus on specific interpretation efforts, we will expand the discussion over possible applications in the conclusive section.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a framework for the semantic alignment of neural units with a complete visual ontology. The proposed method considers semantic relationships between concepts and uses neural circuits to express the units aligned to semantically related concepts.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

(1) Writing: writing is clear and easy to follow

(2) Originality: representing concepts in a structural way is meaningful and many XAI papers consider them as well, e.g.,:

[1] A Peek Into the Reasoning of Neural Networks: Interpreting with Structural Visual Concepts

[2] Interpreting CNN Knowledge via an explanatory graph.

Introducing structural information in Network DIissection is interesting and promising

Weakness:

(1) Lack of baselines, looks like the results do not compare with baseline methods.

(2) Fidelity of the alignment: human-understandable concepts may not be used by CNN during the decision, if the CNN use other decision logic which has no strong relation to the human-defined concepts, then the alignment can not explain the decision of CNN.

(3) Generalization: Could we automatically find the concepts instead of human-predefined? It looks hard in the current setting. If we want to explore the alignment on new tasks (segmentation, detection, VQA) and other datasets, it look we need to create fine-grained annotations for each new dataset/task.

(4) The automatic propagate looks highly aligned with WordNet, how to handle the situation that WordNet structure can not easily maintain in a given dataset. For instance, the dataset may have no label for high-level concepts. For instance, 'animal 'is not a common label, you may need to manually label each of these concepts.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall this is a good paper and easy to follow, I am curious about the answer to the previous questions.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2664 by Reviewer kSuN

content.title: Review Response
content.comment:
*Lack of baselines*

We are currently running additional experiments to compare our framework as closely as possible with the original Network Dissection. We will post a summary of the results as soon as available.

*Fidelity of the alignment*

We agree that the interpretative effort is heavily linked to human-like concept alignment. Many concept-based interpretations of NNs, such as Network Dissection (Bau et al. 2017) or CAVs (Kim et al. 2018), share this limitation. While there is certainly interest in concept-based methods not necessarily aligned to humans, we reserved this concern for future works, but we will cite this in the conclusive section.

*Generalization*

We will explicitly acknowledge techniques to discover visual concepts using non-annotated datasets and their possible integrations with our proposal. Nonetheless, we would like to stress that our framework does not require, in most scenarios, additional labeling effort than the very same supervised labels used to train neural models on the object detection or semantic segmentation task. For instance, we employed an existing bounding-box annotated selection of ImageNet without further labeling. This is a strong and novel point by our approach, afforded by the proposed ontological alignment. 

*Automatic propagation*

In fact, our approach can align units to non-directly labeled visual concepts by exploiting ontological information. By following the example in the comment, even if a dataset does not explicitly annotate the “animal concept”, we will infer from the ontology that existing annotated visual concepts can also be mapped to the more general animal concept. Consequently, we can automatically reconstruct annotations for the general class given its specializations. As a quantitative example of this feature consider Table 1: the non-leaves row mostly accounts for visual concepts that the framework inferred from ontological information, rather than ground truth annotations. For instance, in AlexNet we found several units aligned to high-level visual concepts that were not present in Broden, such as “body of water” (7 units), “geological formation” (6 units), or “garment” (5 units). Finally, we want to specify that we only require an ontology to contain the hypernymy relation and that the adoption of WordNet is thus arbitrary.

content.title: Revision Summary
content.comment:
We thank again all the reviewers for expressing their concerns and offering interesting insights about our work. We uploaded a new revision of the paper, which aims to address the pointed out issues of our proposal. To aid the examination of this new revision, we highlighted with a different color significant changes in the paper. Furthermore, we provide the following summary of the edits:

- *Related works*. We mentioned different concept-based techniques for the interpretation of neural networks that were not originally dealt with. Furthermore, we proposed a possible connection between our work and the task of ontology matching.
- *Ontology-Driven Semantic Alignment*. We included a more formal definition of a semantic relation, which the previous version lacked. Then, we refined Subsection 3.1 and Equation 1 to formally adopt the specialization semantic relation between extensions.
- *Results*. Firstly, we clarified the role of ImageNet to test noisy concept masks. Then, we report a novel comparison with Network Dissection in Table 1, where we offer the results of the IoU metric without considering the automatic propagation of concepts, which we introduced. In this way, the novel data is coherent with the original Network Dissection framework. The table now more precisely shows how our innovations increase the number of retrievable visual concepts. In Figure 3, we included information about the depth of the aligned concepts, to highlight the differences between IoU and our measure.
- *Conclusion*. Our work focuses on the improvement of the semantic alignment between units and human-level concepts. Nonetheless, we included additional information about future research concerning interpretative applications, automatic concept extraction, and not human-understandable visual concepts.
- *Appendix A*. We refined the demonstration of the dependence of IoU on concept popularity, highlighting how our proposal is more fit to address polysemantic units. Furthermore, we included an analysis of the effects of lowering the concept retrieval threshold for both IoU and our measure.
- *Appendix B*. We included a run of the circuit analysis algorithm with the Resnik similarity, to highlight that the approach does not depend on a specific similarity function. Finally, we commented on the results concerning the ImageNet approximated concept masks.
- *Appendix C*. We included a definition of the Resnik similarity.
- *Supplementary materials*. We updated the Jupyter Notebook to replicate the new results in Table 1, Figure 3, and Appendix A. Then, we highlighted how to choose different similarity measures in the implementation of the circuit retrieval algorithm.
